title: Ja'afar the Barmecide and the Bean-Seller

keywords: ja'afar the barmecide and the bean-seller
full_text:
Ja'afar the Barmecide, Grand Vizier to Caliph Harun al-Rashid, was accustomed to walking through the narrow alleys of Baghdad in simple merchant attire to observe the life of the common people. One chilly winter evening, when the icy north wind blew from the mountains, Ja'afar found himself in a desolate lane near the eastern wall, shivering with cold and having missed his evening meal.

Smelling the savory aroma of cooking, he approached a tiny, lantern-lit stall where an old bean-seller named Abu Salih was ladling hot, steaming fava beans into clay bowls, sprinkling them with ground cumin, coarse salt, and fragrant olive oil.

Ja'afar stepped up and searched his pockets, only to discover that he had forgotten his purse at the palace. Embarrassed, the great vizier said: 'Peace be upon you, elder. I am a stranger who has lost his purse; I have not a single copper fals to offer you.'

The old bean-seller smiled warmly, wrapped his coarse woollen shawl tighter, and replied: 'Enter, brother! Food is a gift from the heavens, not a merchandise to withhold from the hungry.' He handed Ja'afar a steaming bowl heaped with hot beans and two fresh barley flatbreads, saying: 'Eat in peace, and warm your bones.'

Ja'afar ate with hearty gratitude, finding the humble meal sweeter than any feast served upon royal gold.

The next morning, royal horsemen rode into the lane, bearing an imperial decree from the Grand Vizier. Abu Salih was brought to the palace, trembling with fear. But Ja'afar descended from his dais, embraced the bean-seller before all the courtiers, and said: 'Yesterday, you fed the hungry without asking for coin; today, the Barmecide repays your bread with gold.'

Ja'afar gifted him a thousand dinars, a comfortable house, and made him the chief provider of grain for the city orphanages, proving that an open heart in a mud stall can outshine the splendor of empires.
moral: Generosity from the humble poor carries more spiritual weight than the lavish gifts of kings.
